questions.title: Synapsis: pairing of homologous chromosomes in prophase I
questions.subject: dev
questions.question: What exactly occurs during the biological process of synapsis in the prophase of the first meiotic division?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sister chromatid separation happens much later, at anaphase II, not during prophase I synapsis, which involves an entirely different pair of structures — homologous chromosomes, not chromatids of the same chromosome.
explanations.B: Correct. Synapsis is the process, specific to prophase I of meiosis, in which each chromosome pairs closely with its homologous partner along its full length, held together by the synaptonemal complex, forming a structure called a bivalent and enabling crossing-over between them. This pairing has no equivalent step in mitosis, where homologous chromosomes never pair with one another at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Division of the cytoplasm (cytokinesis) is a separate, later event that follows nuclear division, not something that occurs during prophase I synapsis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nuclear envelope actually breaks down, rather than condenses, as prophase I progresses toward metaphase I; this is unrelated to the pairing process of synapsis.

questions.learning_objective: Define synapsis as the length-wise pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis via the synaptonemal complex, distinct from any pairing of sister chromatids.
